maintopic: VISIT TO GRANBY, QUE., BY MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT
VISIT TO GRANBY, QUE., BY MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on a question of privilege, I ask your indulgence for a few moments in order that I may bring to the attention of the house what we called the "Marcel Boivin trip."
On Thursday afternoon of last week a party consisting of forty-two members of this house, twenty-one of whom were accompanied by their wives, left Ottawa for a three-day trip to Granby, Quebec, the princess city of the eastern townships. In this group every province of Canada was represented, as well as every political party in the federal field. On arriving at our destination we received a civic reception from the nationally known and dynamic mayor of Granby, Mr. P. H. Boivin, who was accompanied by his charming wife and the members of the municipal council. His Worship remained with us throughout the whole of our stay, and his exuberance, his personality, his wide knowledge of affairs in general, his faith in the future of his city, of his province and of Canada, impressed us very much. He also made us familiar with the great progress already made in that area, as well as its hopes and aspirations for the future, with the inevitable problems that have to be faced and solved.
Numerous and extensive visiting tours were well organized, allowing us to visit several industries, such as the Granby Elastic Web, the Verney corporation, the Miner Rubber Company, the Imperial Tobacco Company, the Granby Co-operative, the Racine Manufacturing Company-just to name a few. Everywhere we were received with courtesy, and we were given the opportunity to make a thorough inspection of these plants in full operation. In the course of conversation it was easy to realize the spirit of co-operation and understanding that exists between labour and management, and at every function both were well represented.
The fine hospitality which is always to the fore in the province of Quebec was manifested by our hosts and by everyone else
with whom we came in contact. I am convinced that all those who made this trip feel that they know more about their country than they did before.
We were inspired by seeing in practice the real unity of the two parent races, and this was at once made evident by the fact that the population of Granby is made up of twenty per cent of English-speaking descent and eighty per cent of French-speaking descent. Its citizens speak the two official languages of our country.
I also wish to express appreciation to the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National for the fine service they gave us, which made our trip a most pleasant and comfortable one.
Before resuming my seat there is another pleasant duty that I wish to perform. I know that in doing so I am voicing the sentiments of my colleagues. It is to present to the hon. member for Shefford (Mr. Boivin), and to Mrs. Boivin, our most heartfelt thanks and appreciation for the very efficient manner in which this tour was organized. The full success of the visit was undoubtedly due to the great care the hon. member took in its preparation, and to his constant presence with his guests. His activities, which made this journey possible, enabled us to see the extraordinary strides that have been made in commerce and industry in his home city. There we met a number of able businessmen, who have contributed their talents and courage in the building up of a prosperous business centre. We also readily perceived that the progress they have made is not attributable only to the efforts of a relatively small group; a large part of the credit must go to the persevering work of the whole population, which is proud of its municipality and anxious to see it progressing in every department.
It will always be with pleasure and gratitude that we shall remember those most agreeable and instructive days.

May I say just a word, Mr. Speaker? I feel sure that all members of the House of Commons will welcome the opportunity to vote for this motion to give effect to the increases and other changes that are set out in the report made by the civil service commission. They are increases that are well deserved, and in many cases long overdue. I shall not make the mistake of referring specifically to any of these that might merit particular attention, because comparisons are unwise to make. I want to express the hope, however, that it will not be long before there will be before the house another report of this kind dealing with employees not covered by this one or by the last one we had, which was laid on the table of the house on April 29, 1948; it is sessional paper 139a of that date.
I could mention one or two of the offices or branches around the building that do not seem to have been considered by way of increases in either of these last two reports. From the study I have made of the various documents in the case, it seems to me that there are still quite a number of subordinate employees who have not had increases that I feel are coming to them. In other words, most of the increases provided for in the report now before us deal with chiefs or assistant chiefs of various branches, although there are included a few subordinate employees who have had a slight upward adjustment.
I want to express the hope-and I am sure that other members will agree with me-that it will not be long before there will be another report of this kind taking care of the needs of some of the other employees. As these changes are made from time to time the employees who are overlooked get the word that their cases will be covered in the next report; then when the next report comes down and they find that they are still not covered, they wonder how long they are going to have to wait.
I fully recognize, Mr. Speaker, the fact that we are dealing in this instance with employees who are permanent and who come under the civil service commission. I fully recognize the fact that this whole business, so far as we have it before us at this time, is beyond the jurisdiction of the officials of the house. It is a civil service matter. When I express the hope that further work will be done on this matter, what I want is that my words and sentiments will be taken note of by the civil service commission, and that they will carry on with the job.

subtopic: COMMUNIQUE ISSUED BY DEFENCE COMMITTEE AFTER MEETINGS AT THE HAGUE

speakeroldname: Hon. Brooke Claxton (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: COMMUNIQUE ISSUED BY DEFENCE COMMITTEE AFTER MEETINGS AT THE HAGUE
speechtext:
Having just returned, Mr. Speaker, from the meetings of the various committees under the North Atlantic treaty which were held at The Hague and were concluded on Saturday night, I thought the house would like to have presented to it the communique issued by the defence committee after it had been approved by the committee at its meeting Saturday evening. It is as follows:
The defence committee of the North Atlantic treaty organization held its third meeting on April 1, 1950, at Juliana barracks, The Hague, The Netherlands, at 10 a.m.
The purpose of the meeting was to consider the work that has been accomplished by the military committee and the military production and supply board since the second meeting of the defence ministers in Paris on December 1, 1949.
The delegates attending the meeting were as follows:
Belgium, Mr. Albert Deveze, Minister of Defence; Canada, Hon. Brooke Claxton, Minister of Defence; Denmark, Mr. Rasmus Hansen, Minister of Defence; France, Mr. Rene Pleven, Minister of Defence; Italy, Mr. Randolfo Pacciardi, Minister of Defence; Luxembourg, Mr. Pierre Dupong, Minister of State; The Netherlands, Mr. W. F. Schokking, Minister of Navy and War; Norway, Mr. Jens Christian Hauge, Minister of Defence; Portugal, Captain Americo Deus Rodrigues Thcmaz, Minister of Marine; United Kingdom, Right Hon. E. Shin well, Minister of Defence; United States, Hon. Louis Johnson, Secretary of Defence.
At the Paris meeting in December the defence committee approved a broad strategic concept which was later adopted by the Atlantic council in January and directed the preparation of plans for the defence of the North Atlantic treaty area.
At its meeting the defence ministers unanimously approved the plan for collective self-defence that was recommended by the chiefs of staff in the military committee earlier in the week.
Within a short space of six months the military planning organization has determined the general strategy of defence of the North Atlantic treaty area, has prepared an estimate of the military situation if any attack be launched against the treaty nations, and has prepared plans for defence against such an aggression should it occur. These plans call for an integrated defence of the entire north Atlantic area as distinguished from individual national defence. Each nation, in accordance with article III of the treaty, will help itself and the others in accordance with its available resources. Thus, for the first time, twelve independent and sovereign nations have achieved, through the democratic process of co-operation, a system for defending themselves and each other.
The defence ministers acknowledged the speed with which the regional planning groups, the standing group and the military committee, achieved the

first basis for their plans. At the same time they directed that the plans be kept under continuous review.
They concerned themselves in particular with the role to be played by the military production and supply board which would insure the most efficient employment of the funds which are appropriated in each nation for military production, and they gave specific directives to this board to implement standardization of equipment and to insure a co-ordinated production.
The defence ministers recognized the great importance of adequate financing to carry out the plan and the need for careful balancing of the respective national economies in the light of the present world situation. For this purpose they requested the defence finance and economic committee to survey the financial and economic potentialities available for defence purposes.
Although considerable progress has been made since their last meeting in the attainment of collective security, which is the common goal of the Atlantic treaty nations, the ministers recognize that further sustained effort will be required. They adjourned with the strengthened conviction that the organization being set up would allow the countries to insure their defence both economically and efficiently.
Mr. Louis Johnson, United States Secretary of Defence, served as chairman of the meeting, and he expressed the gratitude of the committee to The Netherlands government for the kind invitation to meet in The Hague and the hospitality provided.
The time and place for the next meeting will be determined as events require.
That concludes the communique that was approved. I should like to add that in warmth of welcome, hospitality, and the excellence of the arrangements, the government and people of The Netherlands did everything possible for the success of the meeting. Their attitude also showed that the name of Canada still continues to stand high in the hearts and minds of the people and government of that friendly nation.
I should like to say also, Mr. Speaker, that in this connection there is a report appearing in the press of today under a Canadian Press dateline, referring to an Associated Press story, which reads:
The AP story added:
"The Canadians felt they were not getting enough information on technical advances because of a road-block between the Pentagon in Washington and London."
I want to make it perfectly clear that nothing like this was said by any member of the Canadian delegation at The Hague, and that nothing like this was felt. Our arrangements for securing information, either from the United States or from the United Kingdom, in our minds leave nothing whatever to be desired. We are completely satisfied with them. Any suggestion to the contrary is based on a misunderstanding of the situation.
Finally, I should like to say that these meetings at The Hague presented us with an opportunity to discuss with the representatives of the countries there the offer that we had made to their representatives here on the
.	North Atlantic Treaty
16th of March, under which we would train a hundred aircrew and a hundred and fifty army personnel. At The Hague we put before their chiefs of staff memoranda giving details of these proposals, which enabled us to discuss them there; and I have the greatest possible pleasure in telling the house that the reception given to those proposals was very enthusiastic indeed. There is no doubt that with courses that we are giving from June and July on, but mostly starting with the air force toward the end of August and for the army in September, we shall expect to have sufficient applicants, from the various countries desirous of sending officers to train with us, to fill up all the vacancies. It was indicated in the course of our discussion that the plans did give rise to the discussion of rather similar arrangements being developed in other directions; therefore in this we may have started something which may prove to be much larger than the plan itself.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. J. Browne (St. John's West):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when this bill was last before the house I was congratulating the government of

Alberta upon its good fortune in having had such valuable discoveries of oil and natural gas within the boundaries of that province and I was pointing out the increasing use to which these commodities are being put in modern life. Both oil and gas are becoming very popular for household use. There is not a house on the street on which I live in St. John's that does not use oil, and no doubt other hon. members can say the same of their own communities. Within a short time it is likely that oil will completely displace coal as household fuel.
Where there is a large supply of natural gas, as there is in Alberta and Saskatchewan and in many portions of the United States, it seems to be more popular than oil, not only for household but for industrial purposes. Gas has supplanted coal for a number of uses. For a while in Alberta it was used to manufacture gasoline and alcohols and many other by-products. In the field of transportation, from the motorboat of the fisherman to the motorcar of the ordinary citizen, to the great locomotives and even the large steamships, oil is now almost generally supplanting coal.
The importance to Canada of these valuable discoveries can hardly be overestimated. Remarkable developments have taken place within such a short time and are bound to bring with them industrial developments of a scope never contemplated by the government of that province a few years ago.
This is a private bill which seeks certain concessions. It looks innocent enough, but the fact is that it has to do with the transmission of both oil and gas to various places outside Alberta. One wonders why this bill has aroused so much opposition. As I see it, the opposition is due to the fact that there is no provision in the bill which would prevent the promoters or the directors of the company from exporting gas or oil to the United States when the needs of provinces of Canada other than Alberta are not satisfied.
I am aware that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) has said that he has the assurance of the sponsors that they will undertake to have this line built through Canada. If that is so, why should there not be a provision in the bill to that effect? If that provision had been in the bill there would not have been the opposition there has been to this measure.
It has been asked what this bill will mean to the people of eastern Canada. They want to know if it will mean cheaper gas. People are naturally interested in getting cheaper gasoline for their motorcars, cheaper oil for their homes, cheaper gasoline and kerosene for their fishing schooners and motorboats. If the price is to be determined by the supply,
Prairie Transmission Lines and a lot of oil is brought to the surface in Alberta, it will mean reduced importations from the United States, with the result-this has already happened in the prairie provinces -that the price of gas and oil will be reduced for other users.
Transportation by pipe line is much cheaper than by tank car. Anyone requiring gas or oil for domestic or industrial purposes along the route of the pipe line through which gas or oil is being transported will be able to benefit through the decreased cost of transportation. I understand that it will cost 55 cents a barrel to bring oil from the neighbourhood of Calgary to the head of the lakes by pipe line, whereas it costs $1.68 per barrel to transport it by tank car.
Since the last time we discussed this measure I have been reading Industrial Canada to see what the latest news was on the developments in Alberta. I found that the president of the Canadian Manufacturers Association had been holding meetings in different cities in Alberta and had made some important statements about the future of that province and the cities he was visiting. I should like to quote from this magazine, the issue of March, 1950, at page 57, where reference is made to Alberta's oil production. The president of the Canadian Manufacturers Association said:
In this part of the country, however, we have been abundantly blessed in many different ways. Our manufacturing production is increasing. Medicine Hat, rural and urban, has a gross value in excess of $16 million. The Alberta oil and gas industry has already uncovered natural resources worth at least two and one-half billion dollars, despite the fact that it has so far completed only a minute fraction of the ultimate thorough exploration job. This is quickly resulting in the elimination of the greatest single drain on Canada's United States dollar supply and the achievement by Canada of a long term favourable "balance of trade". This augurs well for the future of our well-endowed province.
Speaking at Edmonton, Mr. Carry, chairman of the Edmonton branch of the Canadian Manufacturers Association, said:
... a new wave of prosperity will flood Edmonton district and the west as a result of industrial stimulation provided by oil discoveries.
Mr. East, the national president, said:
... I will not dwell at length on the Alberta oil situation, other than, to say that by and through Alberta's oil production programming, coupled with Alberta's outstanding diversified economy, the future is indeed one of the brightest for any province in the entire dominion.
It is, however, stimulating to all Canadians to pause for a moment to consider the progress made during the last year alone in some of the major enterprises in Edmonton and district. Oil brought more than one hundred new businesses to the city of Edmonton last year, as compared with fifty in 1948. Nine major industrial concerns committed themselves to multi-million dollar construction programs for the year 1950. Four of these projects alone
1478	HOUSE OF
Prairie Transmission Lines
will require Investments In capital construction amounting to about $35 million. Furthermore, about three-quarters of the oil wells in Alberta are in the general Edmonton area. In addition, Edmonton is only forty-five miles from the Redwater field, considered to be the greatest oil field discovered anywhere in the world in recent years.
I have quoted these statements by the president of the Canadian Manufacturers Association to show how important these discoveries are, and how important it is that at the very beginning this development should be conducted along the right lines. According to recent figures, we know that they have discovered in Alberta enough oil and gas to give them a reserve for ninety years. They have seven trillion cubic feet of gas. I should like to point out that that amount of gas is only equal to the annual consumption in the United States. Of course we know that it is only at the beginning so far as Alberta is concerned, but production in Canada is still far behind that of the United States.
I wonder whether anyone has estimated whether it would be better for Canada to export directly from the area around Calgary and Edmonton to the western section of the United States and then carry the gas to Vancouver, and import gas and oil in other areas, or to retain the gas and oil within Canada first and export it from Vancouver to the cities of the western United States. As I understand it, there are four principal steps in getting oil and gas to the consumer. They are-after prospecting -production, refining, transportation and distribution. The other evening I quoted from a book entitled "A National Policy for the Oil Industry." I quote now from page 58:
The struggle over pipe line policy has been going on for several generations. Control of transportation facilities was John D. Rockefeller's key weapon, and the strategic importance of transportation has not declined in the oil industry.
The author goes on to deal with the trouble and confusion into which the oil industry managed to get in the United States because it did not have proper legislation when it began. I believe that the government of the province of Alberta is going to profit by the mistakes made in the United States; but just to show how serious the mistakes might be I should like to point out that it was decided by the Hepburn act of 1906 that pipe lines were common carriers. There was a test of what they could do and what their powers were. The case went to the court and was
[Mr. Browne (St. John's West).!

buried in consideration by the interstate commerce commission. At page 59 the author of the book I have cited said:
After a generation or more of prodding, the interstate commerce commission began its investigation of the petroleum pipe line situation in 1934, and presented its first report in 1940.
That was six years afterwards. The report was not a final order; they reported again in 1944, and that is the last that has been heard of it. It seems to me that it would be a wise course for the country to take the utmost precautions at the beginning of the development to see that legislation governing the transportation of gas and oil is on a sound basis. I believe a Liberal member on this side of the house stated that he was in favour of the bill because the opposition seemed to be in favour of a monopoly. As I understand it, the opposition is not in favour of a monopoly, but favours a policy of safeguarding the interests of the western provinces before gas is exported to the United States. That is a position which everyone can understand, and to which I believe no one in the United States can raise any objection.
The United States have very much larger gas reserves than Canada, and they have oil. The Standard Oil Company of California is one of their largest companies, much larger than all the companies in Canada put together. It is in a position to export oil to the New England states. Therefore the disadvantages which the northwestern states would suffer by reason of not being served first with this pipe line would not be as serious as the disadvantages of the provinces in the western part of Canada if the line does not pass through them.
I agree that gas and oil are commodities which, like water, could be the subject of a monopoly. Not everyone can have a pipe line, although in the United States there are twenty or thirty trunk lines, as well as numerous branch lines. It seems to me that this is the time to insist that the right legislation and the right conditions should be laid down for the transportation of both oil and gas. In connection with another measure of the same sort, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) stated that two sessions ago when it was introduced into the house the promise was made that the company would not export oil to the United States before the needs of Canada were satisfied. He stated the other night that it was because of that promise not being kept, because the line is to be built through the United States, that he is opposed to this bill.
In the last session, in moving the second reading of the bill to incorporate the Alberta Natural Gas Company, the hon. member for

Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Maybank) said he noticed for the first time that the powers sought by the company included the right to export gas outside of Canada. It seems to me that no member, not even a minister of the crown, can give assurances as to what a private company may or may not do. That is laid down by law, and I should like to draw the attention of hon. members to what the law is in this respect.
In the first place I should like to say that there is the Pipe Lines Act of 1949, with which most hon. members are familiar. In my reading of that act, it seems to me there is no power to prevent a company from transporting gas or oil across the border to the United States. In fact, it seems to me that act gives it the power to do so.
According to sections 9, 11 and 12, a company wishing to build a transmission line must make application to the board of transport commissioners, bring in its various plans to show where the line is to be constructed, and if other conditions are satisfactory, it is then entitled' to a permit to construct the line. That, of course, is not the only procedure through which it has to go. Whilst dealing with this act, I should like to draw attention to the difference in treatment between oil lines and gas lines as found in parts II and III of this act. Those who have oil transmission lines may be declared common carriers under section 39, but there is no such provision covering gas lines.
I am aware that, in addition to those provisions governing the matter, there is also the petroleum and natural gas board of Alberta. If a company makes application to that board and receives favourable consideration, the board will report to the government of the province of Alberta, which government would have the last word. The premier of that province has stated a policy, which I think has been read here before, and which briefly consists in prohibiting any export until the needs of the province of Alberta are satisfied, not only its present needs but its long-term needs. After that, if it is satisfied that a surplus exists over and above those requirements sufficient to justify export under sound conservation practices, the government will approve the export of such surplus, with each application being considered on its own merits and in the light of all the prevailing factors. It will be a condition of each export permit that the Canadian requirements must be given priority. The member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) has dealt with that situation, and has pointed out that it may not be considered within the powers of the government of Alberta to say whether or not gas can be exported.
Prairie Transmission Lines
There is on the statute books another act which was brought to our attention by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), the Electricity and Fluid Exportation Act. According to that act the governor in council may make regulations or may grant a licence for export, but I understand the Minister of Trade and Commerce is the one who passes upon that.
I believe I have said sufficient for hon. members to realize that this is a most important subject. The value of this pipe line, not only to the province but to Canada in earning and saving United States dollars, as well as the industries it is going to establish, justifies giving serious consideration to it. I suggest that United States interests will not be jeopardized, and in addition that an examination of the map published in the pamphlet entitled "Natural Gas in Alberta and British Columbia" at pages 10 and 11, would seem to indicate that the chief discoveries in Alberta now centre around Edmonton. The distance a transmission line would have to traverse from there to Vancouver would be shorter than the route through the United States to the cities of Seattle and Portland on the Pacific Coast.
There may be, of course, some reason why it may be more expensive to construct such a line, but I am informed and believe that that route, which has been advocated by so many members on this side of the house, would be preferable to the other route. Other hon. members have argued that the Canadian route will be of special benefit to the cities and towns along its course, and afford those towns opportunities which might otherwise never be given to them. I know that some hon. members are weary of hearing that statement repeated, but is there anything unsound or anything that is not sensible in it? The member for Kamloops has said that if the route does not go through the Kamloops district it is unlikely that gas would be brought up there at any time. Since the advantage of having a gas line to serve these towns is a tremendous one, I believe all hon. members should give serious consideration to the necessity of inserting a provision in this bill to make sure the pipe line does serve that part of the country.
The hon. member for Kamloops also told us of a resolution passed by the British Columbia legislature, to the effect that it would like to see this pipe line go through the province of British Columbia before it goes to the United States. I feel sure the government of the province of Alberta will find it difficult to turn a deaf ear to such a plea. Tf unity in Canada is to have the meaning
1478	HOUSE OF
Prairie Transmission Lines it should have, then a request by the government of one province for such a reasonable measure should meet with a favourable response. If the pipe line is built as requested, it will mean a great deal to the unity and solidarity of the nation. I trust, therefore, that other hon. members will feel, as we do, that this line should go through British Columbia first and may afterwards be conti, nued to the United States. Perhaps the quantity of oil and gas in the province of Alberta will prove so extensive when further discoveries are made that it will be feasible to have another line go south to the United States.
Other features in connection with the construction of the transmission line have not been neglected by previous speakers. The employment provided by the construction of the line, and the furnishing of the pipes, will mean a lot to the people of Canada at a time when unemployment is greater than it has been in any year since before the war. The money will go back into the steel mills and to the iron ore mines. Since the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. Higgins) represents a constituency in which iron ore is found, we trust that industry will receive some benefit.
The other day I noticed an article which spoke of the benefit that would come from the development of the iron ore mines in Quebec. It stated that storage tanks had been built at Seven Islands to contain a million gallons of gasoline. It will be seen, therefore, that all parts of the country benefit from these developments. In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I trust that the Canadian route, which should prove to be popular with all Canadians, and which has been endorsed by the people in the western provinces, will receive the endorsement of hon. members of this house.

The house resumed, from Friday, March 31, consideration of the motion of Mr. May-bank for the second reading of Bill No. 7, respecting Alberta Natural Gas Company, and the motion of Mr. MacDougall: "That this question be now put."

Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank hon. members for having passed the motion, thereby giving me an opportunity to speak on this bill. As hon.
Alberta Natural Gas Company members will recall, at four minutes to nine on Friday night I rose in my place to take part in this pipe lines debate. This will be the fourteenth hour of debate on these pipeline bills during this session.
I said on Friday night that I was in favour of an all-Canadian route. I also said that I thought Canadians were capable of manufacturing the materials for such a pipe line. I think all hon. members would like to see an all-Canadian route. At the same time I believe we are interested, in the debate, in looking at both sides of the picture. I believe Canadians as a whole would like to see their own country helped as much as possible, and I am sure those people residing in British Columbia would like to have this all-important pipe line run through their province, so that industrial and heating facilities may be more readily obtainable.
On Friday last I held in my hand a pamphlet distributed by the Westcoast Transmission Company Limited, mapping a route from Edmonton through to Jasper, through the Yellowhead Pass to Kamloops, with feeder lines to Vernon, Kelowna, Penticton and the great smelter plant at Trail. Then the main line continued on to Hope, Abbotsford and the great city of Vancouver, thence on down the west coast to Bellingham, Everett, Seattle and Portland.
This pamphlet, distributed by the Westcoast Transmission Company Limited, indicates that this is the only company which claims it has constantly sponsored an all-Canadian route to take gas to the Pacific coast. The pamphlet stresses the shortage of United States dollars -a condition which does exist-and that every effort should be made to obtain that route.
The construction of an all-Canadian pipe line will require a large expenditure, and it necessarily follows that the more of the line built in Canada, the more will be spent in this country for its construction. When the gas is sold at the United States border, south of Vancouver, it will command more United States dollars for gas delivered than if the line were built directly south, out of Canada, through a shorter Canadian pipe line.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) stated that this pipe line company have said they have already had Ford, Bacon and Davis, engineers, complete a preliminary survey and design, at this point, for an oil pipe line from Edmonton to Vancouver. Then they propose to follow exactly the same route; and that detailed data and information are now being completed.
1480	HOUSE OF
Alberta Natural Gas Company
It is the hope of all of us that we may see the completion of an all-Canadian route. I believe that at the present time the Steel Company of Canada located at Hamilton, Ontario, is capable of rolling sixteen-inch and eighteen-inch pipe, which is not sufficient in diameter to take care of natural gas. I am informed that, for a line of this type to be successful, at least a thirty-inch pipe is required. There is no doubt that the engineering facilities available here in Canada are sufficient to design such a plant capable of rolling steel here in our own country. I am also informed however that the cost of installing this type of machinery would be about $5 million.
The Westcoast Transmission Company Limited had a bill sponsored in the house some considerable time ago. It was during the dying days of parliament prior to the election of June 27, 1949. An act was passed by parliament on April 30 of that year approving this company's application.
As the pamphlet distributed by the West-coast Transmission Company outlined a Canadian route, it made everything look rosy to anyone reading it. One may look through this pamphlet from cover to cover but one will not find the signature of the president or of any of the directors. I suggest therefore that a pamphlet of this type is nothing but a pure propaganda scheme. The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra is a capable lawyer. I ask him, if he received a pamphlet of this kind, which bore no signature, whether he would accept it as bona fide.
Reference to the statutes of 1949, chapter 36, page 61, shows that a charter was issued to the Trans-Northern Pipe Line Company. Section 6 states:
The company, subject to the provisions of any general legislation relating to pipe lines for the transportation of oil or any liquid product or byproduct thereof which is enacted by parliament, may
(a) within or outside Canada construct, purchase, lease, or otherwise acquire, and hold, develop, operate, maintain, control, lease, mortgage, create liens upon, sell, convey, or otherwise dispose of and turn to account any and all pipe lines, for the transportation of oil including pumping stations, terminals, storage tanks or reservoirs and all works relative thereto for use in connection with the said pipe lines; and own, lease, sell, operate and maintain aircraft and aerodromes for the purpose of its undertaking, together with the facilities required for the operation of such aircraft and aerodromes; and own, lease, operate and maintain interstation telephone, teletype and telegraph communication systems and, subject to The Radio Act, 1938, and any other statute relating to radio, own, lease, operate andi maintain interstation radio communication facilities.
The only company which has applied to construct pipe lines all within Canada is Western Pipe Lines. If hon. members will turn to the 1949 statutes, chapter 38, they will find that under section 6 this company has a charter to build only within Canada.


Then, if we turn to chapter 37 of the 1949 statutes, we find that section 6 deals with the charter given to the Westcoast Transmission Company Limited. This section deals with power to construct and to operate pipe lines, paragraph (a) giving permission to build, as follows:
(a) within the provinces of Alberta and British Columbia or outside Canada-
And I suggest the words "or outside Canada" should be plain enough for anyone-
-construct, purchase, lease, or otherwise acquire, and hold, develop, operate, maintain,-
And so on. May I state clearly again that this company's charter is to build a pipe line either within or outside Canada.
So much time has been taken in debate to show that this company will build in Canada, and that it is the only one that wishes to do so, that I would like the house to know just who these people are. I am taking the words of the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank) who, when he spoke about the Westcoast Transmission Company on November 15, 1949, as reported at page 1811 of Hansard, attempted to show that this company has an all-Canadian charter and is serving Canada's interests first.
This is what the hon. member said, in part:
It has been estimated that It will probably cost $170 million to build the pipe line no matter which company builds it. The money will be raised in Canada and the United States. . . Someone has said something about forty minutes, and I hope it was not a member from British Columbia. I will take my stand right now and vote on the matter as a British Columbia member. Just to show who these people are who are in the Westcoast Transmission Company, may I give you the names of some of the companies in the group. There is the Pacific Petroleums Limited, Calgary, which is a subsidiary. The Peace River Natural Gas Company Limited; Sunray Oil Corporation of Tulsa and Los Angeles- I wish some of my friends would check on these companies. There is the Pacific Western Oil Corporation of Los Angeles and the Tidewater Associated Oil Company of San Francisco. All of these companies have several hundred million dollars behind them. They are the companies through which the Westcoast Transmission Company will finance the undertaking.
As I said before, after their charter was granted, this company made application to build a pipe-line route through the United States. Their application was filed on May 10, 1949. So all the talk of this company wanting to build an all-Canadian route is utter nonsense when section 6 of chapter 37, page 68, of the statutes of 1949, gives this company the right to build within or without Canada. That should be very clear to all hon. members of the house.
There are several routes which this company has applied for through Canada but

which have all been withdrawn. At the moment it seems to me that they are in favour of commencing at Edmonton, going south along the Canadian Pacific railroad to Calgary, then on to Macleod, then west to Pincher Creek and Coleman and through the Crows-nest Pass to Fernie, B.C., leaving Canada at Kingsgate to a terminus at Sandpoint, Idaho, with a branch to Trail, B.C. This application was filed on May 11, 1949, but no action whatsoever has been taken and it has remained dormant since that date. However, it is still on file with the board of transport commissioners and no steps have been taken by the Westcoast Transmission Company to withdraw their application.
The Yellowhead pass route would commence at Edmonton, continue west along the Canadian National main line through Yellow-head pass to Tete Jaune Cache, then southward to Kamloops, Princeton and Vancouver, with a branch line from Tete Jaune Cache to Dawson Creek and a short branch line from Abbotsford near Vancouver to Huntingdon on the United States border. This application was filed on October 13, 1949, and was set down for hearing on November 23, 1949. It was then adjourned at the request of the applicant to February 21, 1950, and again adjourned at the request of the applicant to a date to be set later by the Alberta conservation board to grant a permit to export.
All that parliament is being asked to do is to give these companies now applying for a charter the same opportunity and the same privilege as was given to the Westcoast Transmission Company. We on this side of the house do not believe in monopolies and, therefor, would like to see some competition. In view of the facts that I have stated, will any one suggest that the Sunray Oil Corporation of Tulsa and Los Angeles or the Pacific Western Oil Corporation of Los Angeles or the Tidewater Associated Oil Company of San Francisco are interested in developing Canada first? The answer is, "Certainly not". If the Westcoast Transmission Company are sincere they will make application immediately to withdraw their application to build outside Canada and state clearly that they will follow an all-Canadian route.
I am bringing down a bill entitled, "An act to amend an act to incorporate Westcoast Transmission Company Limited," which reads:
His Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and the House of Commons of Canada, enacts as follows:
1. Paragraph (a) of section six of an act to amend an act to incorporate Westcoast Transmission Company Limited, chapter thirty-seven of the statutes of 1949 (first session) is amended by striking out the words, "or outside Canada," in the second line of the paragraph.

Mr. Speaker, just in order to set the record straight and to satisfy my hon. friends to my left, I want to say that I am not speaking on behalf, or under threat, of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe). Neither am I speaking on behalf of any of the pipe line companies involved in these particular bills. I think we all realize that the time has come to make some decision on this issue. I think it is a fact well recognized that we have wasted considerable time of this house, and I say "wasted" because I mean just that. I know many hon. members will take exception to that word.
Certain hon. gentlemen have led this filibuster. My good friend, the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith), has taken a very prominent part and I must say he has done an able job. When I see examples of his urbane manner and persuasive ways in presenting his viewpoint I begin to feel very sorry for the many jurymen who must have been led up and down various garden paths during his long and distinguished career at the bar.
My good friend, the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank), has also co-operated. While the hon. member probably lacks the great subtlety in the law possessed by the hon. member for Calgary West, he certainly has made up for that lack in the power of his invective. He has done a wonderful job.
Then my good friend, the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green), has been quite prominent in this. I know he has been doing his job in this regard with his customary sincerity. At the same time it struck me that he felt he was leading a second crusade to rescue the Holy Sepulchre from the Saracens. The other night I heard him calling on the shades of senators of the past and present to come and speak in defence of the great people of British Columbia. He also mentioned the gentleman whom I have had the honour to succeed, Mr. A. W. Neill. There is a gentleman who would have made a great contribution to the Senate, but it seems to me that Independents do not often reach that chamber. The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra suggested that if Mr. Neill had been here he would have undertaken to defend British Columbia.
You, Mr. Speaker, were here when my great predecessor was a member of this house and I am sure you will recall that among his many qualities was a great native sagacity and shrewdness. He was a hard .man to whom

Alberta Natural Gas Company to sell a bill of goods and I never heard of him buying any part of the Brooklyn bridge. I am sure that before he would have accepted this gold brick he would have taken a few borings and would have had an assay made so that he would have a pretty good idea whether he should or should not support the bill.
I do not think any of us take second place to anyone else in favouring or desiring an all-Canadian route, but I do not think this house or the committee of the whole is the place to discuss that matter. I am certain some of the hon. members who have spoken do not realize what a highly technical matter this is. There are 60 members of the committee on railways, telegraph lines and shipping and I am sure that many of them are competent to deal with this matter. I am convinced that all those 60 members of that committee will take a close interest in this bill.
I am amazed that the opponents of this bill have appeared so anxious to keep it out of that committee. They seem to me to want to enjoy their own ignorance because I am certain that most of those who have spoken know probably just a little less about pipe lines than I do.
Impossible.

I am sure the hon. member for Calgary West would make a great contribution to that committee. He is not a member of the committee but I imagine when the time comes he will have the Whip have his name replace that of some other member of his party as a member of that committee.
I wonder what has been accomplished by this discussion. It has not all been bad and I would not be unfair enough to say that it has. I think the government has been made conscious of the magnitude of this problem and how interested the people of Canada are in it. I think we have assured ourselves that when the bill goes to the committee it will receive thorough study. It is quite conceivable that as a result of this discussion we have delayed the provision of cheap gas to the Pacific coast by quite a number of months and we may have given the impression to the people of Canada that parliament is being used more or less as a tool to maintain a monopoly for the one company that already has received, a charter from this house.
I feel that any further discussion of this matter is a sheer waste of time. Drawing on my biblical training, and by way of paraphrase, may I say that this house probably will not hold him guiltless who taketh our time in vain. The hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) will probably subscribe to that.

The Westcoast Transmission Company has a charter now. Sometimes I have been annoyed by the tactics they have used. It seems to me that they have played the old shell game on us and have probably taken us for suckers. That is a good Canadian expression and I think it fits. They made a rather feeble and nebulous promise of an all-Canadian route when they came here in the first instance. We saw fit to pass their bill in good faith. In compliance with their promise they applied for an all-Canadian route before the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada on May 10. They are a pretty shrewd and sharp bunch, and it seems to me that they have had some good legal advice. On May 11 they applied for an alternative route for export to the United States. I admire their political skill and vast experience.
I realize that most newspaper reporters do not bother running down to the board of transport commissioners to see what's cooking. They heard that an all-Canadian route had been applied for on May 10, and the Westcoast Transmission Company thought that by shoving the other application through on May 11 nobody would notice it. As a matter of fact, they succeeded very well. The hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) has followed this matter with great interest, but when the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Sinclair) mentioned to the house some four months later than the company had filed an alternative application the hon. member for Calgary West had never even heard of it. He denied it, and I am sure he did so in good faith, because he was not aware of it.
It seems to me it was a shrewd move. It certainly appears to me that the Westcoast Transmission people were not acting in good faith. As to their application for a pipe line permit down through Kingsgate, the Westcoast Transmission people have been wise enough not to embarrass their supporters in the house by asking for a hearing. They are just letting it lie dormant. On the other hand, they withdrew their application for their original plan to build a line from the Athabasca down through Tete Jaune Cache into Vancouver, and they have now replaced it with an application to build a pipe line through the Yellowhead pass about which we have had so much discussion here. On checking with the board of transport commissioners I find they have applied to have that application. adjourned sine die. I am not a lawyer, but the expression "sine die" always strikes me as one of those terms of legal gobbledy-gook that could mean some enchanted evening, when it is springtime in the rockies, or something like that.

A good many of the people connected with the Westcoast Transmission Company are personal friends of mine, but I resented very much the fact that at the beginning of this session they sent us a brochure which had the words on it, "revised, January, 1950". In it they showed a beautiful pipe line route marked all in red through the Yellowhead pass and down to Vancouver. They made sure they did not show that they had made application to go through Kingsgate into the United States. I do not think that people who are asking for these things should try to take advantage of simple-minded members of the House of Commons to that extent.
I have been sorry to hear some of the things that have been said during the course of this debate. In one instance two very prominent and highly regarded people of the province of British Columbia were quoted as being parties to a vicious steal. I think that was a rather unfortunate remark, and I would not like to think that it was made in any derogatory sense. Probably the member was carried away by the enthusiasm of the moment. One of the opponents of this bill has said it, but I certainly would not like to think that the remarks concerning those two gentlemen- and I will not compound the libel by naming them-were supported by other opponents of the bill such as the hon. member for Van-couver-Quadra (Mr. Green) and the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) because I think it would be unfair to suggest that was so.
Some mention has been made in the house of the fact that the legislature of British Columbia passed a resolution supporting an all-Canadian pipe line. It was very good of the legislature of that province to give us gratuitous advice. I think they are expressing the views of most people in the province and certainly of the British Columbia members of parliament. For them to pass a resolution supporting an all-Canadian route is something like my presenting a motion to the house that we are opposed to sin. I think every hon. member would be willing to support me on such a resolution, even some of those who might be interested in trying it.
An editorial in the Vancouver Sun has been quoted extensively. That newspaper has been undertaking to chide some of the Liberal members who have supported the passage of this particular pipe line bill. It seems to me that the editorial department and the news department sometimes get a little mixed up about the direction in which they are going. There is in the press gallery a very able correspondent of the Vancouver Sun, Mr. Dillon O'Leary, and his views do not seem to coincide
Alberta Natural Gas Company entirely with those of the editorial department of the Vancouver Sun. I was particularly interested in one article written on the filibustering debate we had in the house and which appeared in that paper on November 5. Mr. O'Leary starts out by saying:
Mock piety, tear-jerking pleas and lewd humour were part of the weird act in the Commons Friday night during the filibuster in the now famous gas pipe line battle.
Mr. O'Leary is a competent observer, and that appears to be the impression which he, as the man on the job here, gained from some of the debates we have had on this issue. He goes on to say in the article:
Only company holding incorporation for piping Alberta gas to the Pacific coast is Westcoast Transmission Company. Parliamentary sponsors of its incorporation last session, Senator J. W. de B. Farris (Lib., Vancouver) and Mr. Cruickshank have backed moves this session to block incorporation of any other gas pipe line.
To me it is almost humorous to observe the line-up of speakers in this debate. An honourable and distinguished senator is allied with the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank). Then there is the leader of the opposition, the leader of the C.C.F. party (Mr. Coldwell), the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra and the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton). If I have overlooked anybody, all he has to do is to call out his name. It is very interesting. Then we have the resolution of the British Columbia legislature and the comments of the Vancouver Sun, and I understand there are also representations from a number of Liberal organizations in Vancouver Centre. They are all in there together. Pipe-line bills certainly make very strange bedfellows. I know that you will appreciate why I am a little hesitant about getting into bed with that particular crew.
I wonder what we can do with the bill if we give it second reading today. I should like to plead with my hon. friends on this side of the house that we can proceed from here. I do not think any particular harm has been done so far. It seems to me that if the bill is given second reading and is sent to a committee we could very well ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) -and I am sure he would be glad to grant our request-to give us some information on the policy of the Canadian government as to pipe lines. To be fair to him, it seems to me that he has tried several times to provide us with information of that kind, but in almost every instance there has been an attempt to distort his words or to draw from them conclusions that were not fair. I certainly do not have to apologize for anything the Minister of Trade and Commerce

Alberta Natural Gas Company has done. But when it is suggested that he is a party to some nefarious scheme to sell out British Columbia for the benefit of Ontario, I hardly think that is fair. The minister's record since he has been in public life is not one that would indicate it is possible for him to stoop so low; I believe everyone in the house recognizes that.
The building of a pipe line to the Pacific coast is a difficult problem. I know the member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) was stranded on the coast for eight days when, at my invitation, he came there last January. The engineering difficulties connected with the problem of running the pipe line carrying 750 pounds of gas through the Fraser valley must scare him a little. As I have said, I am not an engineer, but I do appreciate the difficulties that are involved. I should like to see these pipe-line experts appear before a committee of the house, and tell us how they can build that pipe line down the Fraser valley to make sure it works every day. We do not want it to be like our railroads that are sometimes out of operation for ten, twenty or thirty days.
As hon. members will probably recall, when this pipe-line proposition was first mooted in Canada I was of the opinion that the Canadian National Railways were passing up a tremendous opportunity that might prove profitable. When I hear Mr. Gordon, the president of the railroad, suggesting that it have a new capital structure, I wish he would present some new ideas about the transportation of gas or oil. I would hope that the government has not entirely abandoned the idea that it might be possible for the Canadian National Railways to get into this business.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would plead wih my friends of the Conservative party, and the C.C.F. party, to allow this bill to go to committee in order that we can get some information on it. So far as I am concerned, I can assure you that if I am satisfied a Canadian route is feasible, both economically and from an engineering standpoint, when this bill comes back for third reading if there is any way I can assist in ensuring the pipe line will be built in Canada, I shall support those hon. members requesting that route, and not the pipe-line company that wishes to go through the United States.

Mr. Speaker, since a very important principle is involved, it should surprise no one to see Quebec members rise and speak, after many others, against the bill respecting the Alberta Natural Gas Company.


Mr. Speaker, may I say at once that I am amazed, even shocked, at the attitude shown by certain Liberal members since we began discussing this private bill concerning the Alberta Natural Gas Company. Of course, some may ascribe my surprise to inexperience. This, indeed, is only my second session and I still have a lot to learn. One thing, however, that is very well known to me, even if I lack the long experience of most of my colleagues, is the feeling of my constituents and, may I add without boasting, the feeling of most of the people in my province.
The people of Labelle county and of the surrounding constituencies find it strange that members of parliament are always tempted to surrender to commissions and bureaucratic bodies their authority and prerogatives, as well as the rights and duties of their office. The bill concerning the Alberta Natural Gas Company is a good1, or rather a deplorable example, of a state of affairs about which the people are complaining bitterly.
It. is our duty as members to examine this bill. This means we should have some knowledge, some information about this matter. It is not sufficient to vote for or against the bill, once the title has been read. We must know what is involved. Liberal members are willing to approve the measure immediately, without even taking into account its implications. When we censure this attitude, they say: "If anything goes wrong, the board of transport commissioners will deal with it". Indeed, the board will look after it. Having become nothing but rubber stamps, the members vote blindly. When it is time to decide, to judge, to take a definite line of action, the move is made by bureaucrats, commissioners, or someone else. The board of transport commissioners is not to blame in any way. But the principle involved is very important.
The Alberta Natural Gas Company has applied for a charter to build pipe lines. According to the law, members of the house can grant or, if they see fit, deny the charter. We, the Conservative members of the opposition, naturally ask, and it is nothing more than our duty to inquire, what route these pipe lines will follow. No answer has been given. Can we, the representatives of the people, grant the charter notwithstanding, saying, with the Liberals, that if anything goes wrong, the board of transport commissioners will see to it? No, there are cases where, under the law, it is up to the board of transport commissioners to assume its responsibilities. In this instance, however, the members of this house

must acquit themselves of their obligations. We find it strange, I repeat, that they fail to do so.
If ten or fifteen years hence we should find out that these pipe lines follow such a route that they do not favour Canadian interests, or that they even are contrary to them, who will be held responsible? The board of transport commissioners? What use would that be since the members of this board are not elected by the people? The members of parliament themselves would be held to blame, and rightly so, since we would have neglected, when the moment came, to carry out our duties as representatives of the people.
Even government supporters are sometimes heard to complain that the members of this house are too often ignored when the time comes to make an important decision or to acquaint the people with an order in council or other such orders.
In October, 1949, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) was the first to be surprised on reading in certain newspapers about the statement he intended to make in the House of Commons. That statement dealt with the setting-up of controls on imports of certain goods such as pig iron, iron ingots, billets, bars, rod, et cetera. Members of the house were not informed of this order yet the news was already published in the press and known to the general public. Busy with their parliamentary duties, the members were the last to be informed. I have a great deal of admiration for newspapermen and I was highly amused to see that they had scooped the members of the House of Commons. Besides, in this particular case, the incident was not of major importance. However, it enabled us to realize once more that a very dangerous tendency exists. No longer do members of parliament, the elected representatives of the people, administer public affairs; bureaucrats, high officials and some not so high, who, nevertheless have been given impressive powers, now crack the whip.
We know that a good many Liberals do not like that procedure; they do not want to be informed of tax increases or reductions through the medium of the radio or the press. Here is a wonderful opportunity for them to prove that they are sincere by refusing to entrust their responsibilities to the board of transport commissioners or to the government 55946-95i
Alberta Natural Gas Company of Alberta. By acting otherwise, they let most dangerous precedents pile up, and some day we may awake to find out that a board of some kind has simply decided to abolish parliament. That may seem fantastic, but the representatives of the people are surrendering their authority to civil servants at such a rate that we can very well expect the worst.
I was also rather surprised to see the Liberal members attach only minor importance to the conservation of our natural resources. In opposing the bill concerning the Alberta Natural Gas Company, we seek only to protect our natural resources. Given a free hand, the company would be in a position to deal with the oil and gas resources of Alberta in its own interest, which may be detrimental to the interests of the country as a whole, and according to its own whims which may be prejudicial to the whole population.
We have no right to authorize a company to use our natural resources as it sees fit. We should first know exactly about the company's intentions, its plans and projects, and then prescribe conditions based on the most elementary caution. Because we ask questions, because we want to know, for instance, what route the Alberta Natural Gas Company's pipe lines will follow, we are taxed with shameful intentions.
We should do everything in our power to favour the development of our natural resources in the interest of our people at large. Such development should be carried out systematically. Oil resources, as has been shown elsewhere, are not inexhaustible. Should we, therefore, let this company export, large quantities of oil to the United States and then find, in a few years, that Canada's reserves of that precious fuel are exhausted? Hon. members know that the province of Quebec has abundant natural resources. We realize, however, that they cannot last forever and that unrestricted development could well entail serious disasters, economic and otherwise.
Take, for instance, the case of the paper' industry. In our province, we have vast forests. Some people would doubtless be-tempted to process all this timber into newsprint as fast as possible so as to make all the-money they can! To do so would be illogical. We must think of the future. A forest can be denuded in a few weeks, but it takes years
