Alberta Natural Gas Company and years to reforest land. That is why in our province we make sure that forest development is carried out systematically and carefully; we also see to it that reforestation goes hand in hand with deforestation. That is but elementary foresight. No generation has the right to strip land of all its natural resources in a manner that would leave future generations in want.
What goes for forests also applies to oil. Previous speakers have told us how valuable, how useful petroleum and natural gas are to us Canadians; they have mentioned all the benefits we can derive from these assets. "Black gold" it is sometimes called, and rightly so.
Besides, the oil industry is a relatively recent one, not only in Canada but throughout the world. It might be pointed out that it began less than a hundred years ago. On August 27, 1859, Edwin Drake was digging an artesian well in his garden-a rather commonplace occupation-when suddenly oil spurted out from the bowels of the earth. This incident occurred at Titusville, Pennsylvania, in the United States. Good old Drake, a common bartender, died a colonel and, what is more important, a multimillionaire. The rest is history: there was a rush of oil prospectors. Men had found the black gold Eldorado".
Oil has revolutionized industrial processes. One need not be a prophet to state that still further changes and industrial revolutions will be caused by oil. In December, 1938, the late President Roosevelt stated:
Oil has become the sinews of war.
Nineteen years earlier Clemenceau had cabled Wilson the following message:
Each drop of oil is worth a drop of blood. We have been carried to victory by a flood of oil.
Beyond any doubt, oil has played a vital role in the last two world wars. Supremacy in this field meant supremacy on land, on sea and in the air. In Napoleon's time, an army marched on its stomach. While this remains true, it also marches on oil.
We have here the annual report submitted by Imperial Oil Limited for 1944; it was published in Sarnia, Ontario, on April 14, 1945.


The following significant passages deal with the accomplishments for which oil has been responsible:
The year under review has been yet another period during which the resourcefulness, courage and wealth of the United Nations have been put to the test in preserving individual liberty and a democratic way of life. While peace-loving nations accumulated material and took the offensive on the main theatres of operations, oil has been called upon to play an increasingly important part in every phase of the war effort, on the battle front as well as on the production front. Briefly, there has been an enormous demand for crude petroleum and its products, vast movements of oil and allied products over long distances, adaptation of these products to new uses and a development of new products with a view to fulfilling special requirements of navies, air forces or land armies, war industries and other essential uses.
In spite of difficulties, it can be said that in Canada once again, in 1944, no convoy was delayed, no movement of troops was hindered, no flying field was closed and no production of munitions, food or other essential products was curtailed on account of a shortage of oil supplies.
These few sentences show us the importance of oil in wartime. I am not one of those who believe that Canada should engage in gigantic preparations in case we should have a third world war. I am not one of those who believe that the major part of the revenue of the federal government should go towards the purchase of munitions. I do think however that if we really treasure our security and our independence, we must not let the development of our oil resources take place in a haphazard way. In peacetime as in wartime oil plays a vital part, but in wartime it can be essential to victory.
We are therefore clearly against the irrational use of our natural resources, and the irrational export of the products of our resources. We use the word "irrational" since this bill gives no guarantee that the use and export of our resources will be on a rational basis. It is our duty, as members of this house, to oppose the passing of a bill which provides no such guarantee. For reasons already mentioned, we cannot devolve upon the board of transport commissioners or the Alberta government responsibilities incumbent upon us.
Should we grant its application, the Alberta Natural Gas Company would have wide powers, extraordinary powers. The

Pipe Lines Act of April 30, 1949, clearly defines such powers. We would allow the company, among other things, to-
-enter into and upon any crown land without previous licence therefor, or into or upon the land of any person, lying in the intended route of its line, and make surveys, examinations or other necessary arrangements on such land for fixing the site of the line, and set out and ascertain such parts of the land as are necessary and proper for the line;
But we members of this house who are going to allow this company to construct pipe lines, do not even know what route is going to be used or what crown lands those lines will enter upon without previous licence. Nor do we know upon what lands belonging to individuals, to taxpayers, will the same liberty be taken.
Under the terms of the act the company may also; . . . purchase, take and hold of and from any person any land or other property necessary . . .
... or dispose of any of its land or property that for any reason has become unnecessary for the purpose of the line.
Here again we cannot, as the people's representatives, give them a free hand without knowing beforehand at least the route of the pipe lines.
The act passed on April 30, 1949, provides many other extensive powers including the following:
. . . construct, lay, carry or place its line across, upon or under the land of any person on the located line of the company pipe line.
They will not tell us where the line will go, but still they want us to agree to everything they ask for.
The act continues:
Join its line with the pipe line of any other person at any point on its route.
Always a route about which we know nothing at all.
Construct, erect and maintain all necessary and convenient roads, buildings, stations, depots, wharves, docks and other structures, and construct, purchase and acquire machinery and other apparatus necessary for the construction, maintenance and operations of its line.
Construct, maintain and operate branch lines, and for that purpose exercise all the powers, privileges and authority necessary therefor, in as full and ample a manner as for a company pipe line.
Those are rather sweeping powers which we are being asked to grant without being able to get beforehand the information we ask for.
Let us read the act further, especially the different paragraphs of the important section 7:
. . . from time to time alter, repair or discontinue the works or any of them, mentioned in this section, and substitute others in their stead;
Alberta Natural Gas Company
Transport oil or gas by company pipe-line and regulate the time and manner in which oil or gas shall be transported, and the tolls to be charged therefor; and
Do all other acts necessary for the construction, maintenance and operation of its line.
Indeed, we should not grant all of these powers and privileges before knowing the truth about this venture, the route to be followed by the proposed pipe line or pipe lines, whether the oil and gas to be carried in this or these pipe lines will remain ini Canada or enter the United States and what percentage will remain in this country and what percentage, if any, will be exported to the United States.
Charity begins at home. We need oil and gas here in Canada, especially in the western provinces. Our people should be the first to benefit from our oil and gas resources. If there is a surplus, let us export it; it would be to our mutual advantage. On the other hand, it would be perfectly ridiculous to hinder the development, progress and prosperity of a section of our country by depriving it of oil and gas in order to export those products to the United States.
The hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Murray) said something like this:
Some people fear our southern neighbours as if they were ready to jump on us.
Let us be serious please! We admire our southern neighbours; we have great friendship ties that unite us and we are proud of the undefended border between our two countries. We do a great deal of trade with the United States. The friendly relations between our two nations are an inspiring example for the rest of the world. Washington, however, has never asked Ottawa to deny itself completely, to forget its immediate or remote interests and to sacrifice itself in any way on behalf of the United States. Neither has Canada ever demanded that Washington set aside its own interests to think only of Canada's.
The Hyde Park agreement of 1941 does hot state that Canada must deny herself completely to consider only the United States. Let us see, for instance, how, in 1942, the United States Secretary of State outlined what we should aim at in taking steps to ensure economic co-operation; he said something to this effect:
. . . co-operate in working out a common program in which all other countries sharing the same ideas would be invited to take part in order to increase,

Alberta Natural Gas Company
toy means of the international and internal steps deemed necessary, production, employment as well as the exchange and consumption of goods, those being the material bases of the freedom and welfare of all peoples.
Nothing more. It is not contemplated that we should do without essential products in order to export them to the United States, nor, for that matter, is it inferred that the United States will make every necessary sacrifice in order to send to Canada goods that are in short supply. Complete and frank co-operation between Ottawa and Washington, by all means, but never, however, to the disadvantage of either Ottawa or Washington. Otherwise, the end to be achieved would no longer exist.
Let us suppose, for instance, that only enough oil was found in Alberta to supply the people of the neighbouring provinces. Now these provinces need oil badly and this product can ensure their prosperity. Under what principle or precedent can we ask the citizens of Alberta, of British Columbia or of any other province to do without oil or gas in order that we may export it to our neighbours to the south? Let me repeat that charity begins at home, as the saying goes. This principle applies both in personal relations and international relations. Besides, the United States have never asked us to deny ourselves oil and gas to provide them [DOT]with these products. Let us not ascribe to them intentions they do not have.
If a similar bill were to be introduced in Washington, there is no doubt that, first and foremost, it would be designed to protect United States interests. The representatives of the American people would not allow oil to be exported to Canada unless they were assured that the United States had enough for their own needs. Nobody in Ottawa could be shocked by such an attitude. It would be judged to be quite normal and reasonable. However, Liberal members-not all, but a few-would have us believe that it would be different if representatives of the Canadian people were to do the same.
The member for Skeena (Mr. Apple-whaite) seemed quite put out because we of :the Conservative opposition were not of one mind with him. He waxes indignant-and these are his very words-because, as it were:
The suggestion has been made that we who support these bills . . .
That is, the Liberal members.
. . . are in some way traitors to Canada or to our respective provinces.


The member for Skeena may be annoyed but he knows very well that he is duty bound, as a member of this house, to proceed
with caution and foresight whenever a bill is considered. The member who casts a vote for any bill without due consideration is not being faithful to his mandate; he betrays it. In supporting a measure such as the Alberta Natural Gas Company bill, the implications and consequences of which he is totally unaware, he is apt, voluntarily or not, to betray the interests of his province, of his country. One may betray by doing certain tilings; one may also betray by omitting to do certain things. By neglecting to examine thoroughly the purposes of the Alberta Natural Gas Company we would, in effect, betray our mandate, our electors and our country.
If, indeed, there is nothing to fear, if everything is in the best interest of the country, why not then provide the information we request in good faith?
The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Maybank) moved second reading of the bill. It is of him therefore that we asked: "What route will the pipe line follow?" That surely is a fair question and we would be remiss in our duty as members of this house if we did not ask it. The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre replied: I do not know.
How can we grant extraordinary powers to a company, if we do not even know what route its pipe line will follow, to whom the company will sell the oil, whether it will serve Canadian or American customers first or whether it will take no interest in either of them. We are completely in the dark in that connection. The more we progress, the more we discuss the matter, the more we realize that it would be beyond our power to authorize the Alberta Natural Gas Company to go ahead with projects of which we know nothing. Would the company work against the interests of the nation or those of a particular province? We like to think that such are not its intentions. However, for the very reason that we do not know what it plans to do, we can assume all sorts of hypotheses, some good, some bad, and think the best as well as the worst.
The members of the house should be in a position to tell the Alberta Natural Gas Company what route its pipe line must follow

in the nation's interest; however, not only are we prevented from correcting or altering the plans of the company but we do not even know what route it will follow.
We are told that the board of transport commissioners will deal with this. It will probably attend to the matter from the technical standpoint, from a specific angle, but its attitude will not be that of a member of the house, a representative of the people. I am loath to see members of parliament always surrendering their rights, powers, prerogatives and responsibilities to others.
There is also the government of Alberta, we are told. They will see to that. They will take steps to protect the interests of the province of Alberta. That is quite normal and is to be expected. But will they make sure that the interests of British Columbia are also protected? We know, of course, that they will not. We are well aware that it is here, in this house and nowhere else, that the general interest, the interests of the country at large will best be protected.
Finally, the Department of Trade and Commerce has been mentioned. By the Department of Trade and Commerce, do they mean the high officials, the powerful bureaucrats? If these are the people referred to, our answer is no, a thousand and ten thousand times no. At the beginning of my remarks, I voiced the opinion of the party with respect to federal bureaucracy and its activities. That applies to the bureaucrats of the Department of Trade and Commerce as well as to those of all other departments. Even if such were the case, our answer would still be no. We have listened to the speeches and statements made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce and they were hardly reassuring.
For instance the member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank) has already asked him if we may conclude from a statement which may be found at page 792 of Hansard whether no export permit would be granted for oil if the suggested pipe line were not entirely within Canada. The answer given by the Minister of Trade and Commerce was so vague that the member for Fraser Valley had this to say:
I take it that the minister is not going to answer my question?
The Minister of Trade and Commerce had a word for those who oppose the export, or at least the unrestricted export, of Canadian oil to the United States. He called them "petty Canadians". We do want to be those "petty Canadians" who look first to their own country's interests and have no wish to favour foreigners over our own taxpayers. We do
Alberta Natural Gas Company not mind being those "petty Canadians" who are heedful of the unfortunate consequences of a blank cheque-for that is what is being requested of us-given to the company which intends building this pipe line.
We want to be "petty Canadians" who consider, above all, the present and future of their own country and secondly, secondly only, the interests of others, of our neighbours. I repeat, Mr. Speaker, charity begins at home!
Therefore, whatever may be the intention of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, we will not let him decide alone, or with his advisers or bureaucrats, what the route of the Alberta Natural Gas Company pipe line should be. The Minister of Trade and Commerce is a busy man. He must have other matters to attend to. The members will want to settle among themselves a problem which concerns them in the first place. Besides, the Minister of Trade and Commerce is sufficiently powerful; he does not need any more privileges or prerogatives. We know he is used to government by order in council. We of the Conservative opposition do not like it at all. We believe in the sovereignty of parliament and we shall express our belief on all occasions, in this matter of the Alberta Natural Gas Company and in any other.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce, who is a very busy man, which is quite understandable, is sometimes absent-minded. Need I, for example, recall that on December 6 last, the minister clearly denied that Canada had shipped uranium to Soviet Russia? Two days later, on December 8, he admitted in the Commons-

The house resumed at eight o'clock. PRIVATE BILLS

The house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Maybank for the second reading of Bill No. 7, respecting Alberta Natural Gas Company, and the motion of Mr. MacDougall: "That this question be now put."

In
rising to speak again in this debate, Mr. Speaker, I make no apology because I believe I am representing the views of the majority

of the people of the province from which I come and, without question, the views of the majority of the people in the constituency which I have the honour to represent. I think that is evidenced by the fact that the legislature of British Columbia has unanimously adopted a resolution in support of an allCanadian route for a pipe line through British Columbia. In addition to that, I have received, as have many other members from British Columbia, a large number of resolutions from boards of trade and other service organizations, and also resolutions from trade union organizations, representatives of the various trade union congresses in British Columbia, and other public service organizations. Without any doubt whatever, I think that what we who are speaking in opposition to this bill as now presented to the house have to say are the words that thousands of people in British Columbia would have to say if they had the opportunity to be here to give voice to their opinions.
Before proceeding with my somewhat brief remarks this evening I want to say again that I make no apology for speaking in this debate. Like other hon. members who have spoken, we know nothing of the personnel behind these companies. We know nothing about the companies as such; that is, their personnel, their structure and so on. Personally, I know nothing of the eminent counsel who are supposed to be interested in these bills, according to the remarks of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Gibson) this afternoon. All we are doing here is giving voice to a principle. That principle is that we believe that whoever receives a charter, or whatever companies receive charters to build pipe lines, should first give this house their assurance that Canadian requirements and Canadian communities will be served before any such pipe line enters the United States.
The members from British Columbia, representing all parties from British Columbia, who have spoken in this debate against these bills as presented at the present time, appreciate the assistance they have received from members of other provinces. We appreciate the assistance we have received from the Ontario members who have been big enough to take an all-Canadian .approach to this, to us, important question. Order. Again I must remind hon. members that they must not interrupt the hon. member who has the floor.

I have very little idea of the amount of gas that may be produced in Alberta, but I do know that if some hon. members would only stop to think they would get some information into their heads. I was talking to a couple of local members and they had not even read the bill. Yet they thump their desks and make a lot of noise in here.
This pipe line will develop the United States. What I am fearful of is that this part of the United States will develop so fast when they find out that they are going to get gas that it will be to the detriment of British Columbia and Alberta. When the pipe line is under construction houses will convert their heating systems to use gas, industries will be developed all along this pipe line with the use of gas. I am fearful that very little gas will ever get back into Canada to be used in Vancouver or in any part of British Columbia. You will get only what is left after the other fellow is through with it.
I do not want to deprive the United States people of anything, but I do want to see Canadians get the benefit of this utility first. I have many friends in the United States; I have business associates there. Hardly a month goes by that I do not do business with some United States firm or some individual in that country. But every time a citizen of the United States gets a concession he never relinquishes it. I know that in my own business back in 1922 United States lumber wholesalers said to us: "We are going to buy your lumber at 2 per cent, 30 days." Previous to that time they used to pay cash and never more than 30 days. They said:	"We are
going to buy your lumber at 2 per cent, 30 days." We accepted, yes. We accepted it like the fellow on the street who walks up to another man and puts a gun to his ribs and says:	"Give me your watch." The United
States was the only market we had at that time, other than the Canadian market. It was the only place to which we were exporting. These people still hang on to that concession. They have hung on to it through good times and bad. They have never relinquished their hold on that set-up in the lumber business. Even during the war they still hung on to it. The hon. member for Comox-Albemi, who is a lumberman, knows that what I am saying is true.

We like that business.

Alberta Natural Gas Company

It is a good business, but we would rather have it cash, 30 days, and not 2 per cent, 30 days. When you consider that 2 per cent, it amounts to 12 per cent per annum, which is not a bad profit in itself. It is no fault of the people of the United States. That is their way of doing business. They would not think any the less of us if we protected ourselves first. It is possible for us to protect ourselves in any business, and they will not think any the less of us. They will still do business with us, I am sure, if Canada takes care of developing her own natural resources for the benefit of Canadians first. No citizen of the United States will think any worse of us if we do that. They would still have a friendly feeling toward us. They will be glad to take what is left over after our needs have been supplied rather than have Canadians take what is left over.
Just recently the Canadian National Railways sold their mineral rights in a lot of property in the western provinces. I think they should have held on to them for this very same reason. There is going to be natural gas and oil produced or found in that area, and a pipe line will be needed to transport it. It will certainly be transported by pipe line when it is discovered in large enough quantities to warrant such a line.
I think it was a mistake. 1 am not so enamoured of private enterprise that I cannot see the need for national undertakings at times. Probably that may sound a little bit socialistic, but it would be to the benefit of Canada. The Canadian National Railways are operated in that way. The Ontario hydro is handled in that way. The other day the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) spoke about Polymer. He said that was his enterprise, and that he was proud of it. He should be proud of it. He is proud of it, and rightly so. If we have to grant charters, if we have to give away natural resources, to get somebody to put up a few dollars to build a pipe line, then I think the government of Canada should build a pipe line itself. It is a national enterprise. It is something that is ot going to just one province. Eventually it will go through the United States. I would be satisfied if the government had gone so far as to say that it would build this pipe line and have it owned by Canadians, for Canadians, and for our future generations.
Anyone who looks through the list of bills which have been passed in earlier sessions of parliament, particularly in the one last spring, will see bill after bill introduced by private members in which they have asked for things which would be all-Canadian. They have wanted this thing or that thing to be Canadian, and their wishes have taken different


forms. I have no doubt many of the things for which they have asked would have been beneficial.
However, I would ask those same members, the members who signed those bills, who sponsored them and followed them through the house, to think commercially for Canada for a few moments. Let them make up their minds how they will vote on this question. Let them decide whether they want something that is all-Canadian, or something that is tied to the United States or to some other country.
I believe all hon. members will agree that, from the standpoint of defence, we can appreciate our hook-up with the United States. We appreciate, too, our commercial position in relation to that country. At the same time, as Canadians we must look first to the development of our natural resources, for Canadians.
In his speech the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Applewhaite) said, as reported at page 901 of Hansard:
What about the consumer? Have we no responsibility for the consumer? I assume every hon. member will agree that the final cost to the consumer must depend very largely upon the cost of the capital works involved. And this brings me to a reiteration of a statement that I have made before, that we all favour the principle of an all-Canadian route. Why on earth would we not? But not if such a route is going to have the result of materially adding to the costs of home owners and the costs of production for ever to those who want to use gas as fuel or as power.
Mr. Speaker, there is one thing to be said, and that is this, that there will not be any Canadian consumers in British Columbia if this route goes down to the south. If it goes through the Yellowhead pass and the interior of British Columbia it will serve the Canadian consumer in British Columbia and other parts of western Canada.
Then, so far as price is concerned, I do not think there is any member who can tell what the cost of this route will be. Even if it did cost a few dollars more, taking for granted that the Yellowhead route might be more expensive-and I doubt if it would-but even if it did cost a little more, the Canadian consumer would reap the benefit. Even if it cost one or two cents more per month to heat his home, is it not better for him to have that service and to save perhaps $100 in a season, the difference between heating by coal and by gas? It is much better to pay a few cents a month more than to have to heat his house with wood or coal.
Like many other members, I am the father of a family, and I look to the future of Canada and to the younger generation coming along. I say to hon. members that I am most anxious to do my part to build a better Canada for all young Canadians so that they may find

employment, so that this country may be developed, and so that future Canadians will be able to look back, in the years to come, and realize that those of us who are here today have builded better than we knew.
Many new members have come to the House of Commons in the last election. They seem to have learned fast. Among them are some bright gentlemen, and I have been pleased to meet them and to accept them as my colleagues. But they have developed into the greatest desk thumpers we have ever seen in the House of Commons in the last five years. That trait has developed quickly, and they seem to hang on to it. Hon. members will recall the way they went after me when I began my remarks. Of course, I did not mind, because one must be prepared for that in the House of Commons. If that is what they think they are here for, and if they are pleased about it, then I shall be pleased too. But let me say this one word to them: Do not forget that, no matter what happened in Canada before, you are the heirs of the past; you are the trustees of the future. Think that over before voting on this question.
We are approaching the Easter recess, and the debate on this matter has been lengthy. Perhaps there will be more of it. However, I think it would be well if all hon. members had the opportunity to go back home and talk this over with their constituents before attempting to decide the issue here. It is not going to take much more time to wait until after the Easter recess for the vote.
Therefore, seconded by the hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Catherwood), I move the adjournment of the debate.

When a similar motion was made earlier this evening I raised the question as to whether it was in order to move in succession two motions to adjourn the debate, without an intermediate proceeding. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) rose to discuss the matter. Then I decided that since there had been an intermediate proceeding the point of order did not arise.
At this time, however, I should be glad to hear any hon. member on the question as to whether a motion to adjourn the debate can follow a similar motion, without an intermediate proceeding.

As I suggested then, standing order 48 is the one that makes provision for a motion to adjourn the debate. It reads:
When a question is under debate no question is received unless to amend it, to postpone it to a day certain; for the previous question; for reading the orders of the day; for proceeding to another order; to adjourn the debate; or for the adjournment of the house.
It is to be noted, of course, that if there are any other standing orders that limit the application of this standing order, they have to be taken into consideration. Your Honour therefore raised the question as to the meaning of standing order 30, in its relation to standing order 48. Standing order 30 reads:
A motion to adjourn (except when made for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance), shall always be in order, but no second motion to the same effect shall be made until after some intermediate proceeding has been had.
Two questions arise, the first of which is this: Is a motion to adjourn the debate covered by standing order 30, which specifies a motion to adjourn? And, secondly, what is an intermediate proceeding?
We turn to citation 164 in Beauchesne's third edition, and find this paragraph:
The term "intermediate proceeding" used in standing order 30, means a proceeding that can properly be entered on the Journals. The true test is that if any parliamentary proceeding takes place, the second motion is regular, and the clerk ought to enter the proceedings to show that the motion in question is regular. It is usual to alternate motions for adjournment of house and debate when a question is under consideration.
And then follows the notation "B.322,323" which, of course, indicates that that citation was taken from Bourinot's fourth edition, at pages 322 and 323. As a matter of fact the quotation which Beauchesne gave from Bourinot has been altered slightly, but not to change its meaning, except in so far as part of it has been omitted. I should like to quote the rest of that paragraph from Bourinot where he says:
The true test is that if any parliamentary proceeding takes place, the second motion is regular, and the clerk ought to enter the proceedings to show that the motion in question is regular. It is usual to alternate motions for adjournment of house and debate when a question is under consideration. In case there is a substantive motion of adjournment before, the house, and it is negatived, some proceeding must be had in order to render a second motion to the same effect regular.
I pause to emphasize that the reference there is to a substantive motion of adjournment. I go on:
A message from the governor general followed by other proceedings would be sufficient to render a second motion of adjournment valid.

The rule applies literally to the adjournment of the house, and not of the debate-
In other words, Bourinot quite clearly says that when it is a motion to adjourn the house, the rule must be applied literally and some other proceeding must intervene, but that the rule does not apply when it is a motion to adjourn the debate. Let me read the whole sentence:
The rule applies literally to the adjournment of the house, and not of the debate, but it is usual and convenient to make an entry in the Journal between two motions of the latter character.
In other words, between two motions to adjourn the debate there should be an entry in the Journals to show that something has happened in the meantime. That paragraph ends with a reference to a footnote (u) which refers to a number of instances in Hansard of bygone days. The instance that occurred on June 22, 1891, was a case where there had to be some intermediate proceeding of another character because on that occasion the two motions were motions to adjourn the house. Alberta Natural Gas Company them to fill it up; and it has not gripped investments sufficiently to develop it to the extent that it will be developed.
As I sit here and see in my mind's eye the map of the world, and contemplate the world's potentialities, I realize what a privilege I have had in going round the world and seeing what has happened to oil in other places, and what oil and gas will do for a community. Glendavis in Australia, and the state of New South Wales, a few years ago put up 666,000 Australian pounds, matched by the Commonwealth of Australia; and some of my associates whom I learned to love and admire put up a like amount to make 2 million Australian pounds sterling in 1941, 1942, 1943 and 1944. For what purpose? They lacked in Australia, and this is true of New Zealand as well, oil and gas with which to develop the country and to defend themselves in the last great war. They depended entirely on the United States of America. So those three organizations banded themselves together and what did they do?
When they found the predicament they were in, they checked the whole Commonwealth of Australia and found some shale deposits which had a bearing of oil, not to the same degree as has been found in Estonia, now behind the iron curtain, but still a certain bearing of oil. They banded themselves together because there was a war on and oil 'was vital to their existence. They were not sure whether the United States-Texas and the other states-could provide them with sufficient fuel to protect themselves.
I do not know whether my next sentence should be uttered, but now that the war is over I think I may say it is common knowledge that, finding themselves in that predicament, without oil and without gasoline, and without gas to propel their protective devices of one kind and another, they drew their defence lines back from the north part of Australia to a point close to the centre line of the country, with a view to making a last stand when that was necessary. But, thank God, the United States and the allied nations were able to keep pumping oil and fuel into that country of theirs and they were able in that remote part of the world to defend themselves.
When the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) rises in his place and says that, for our self-preservation and protection, we should not give away this natural resource which Providence has given us, I have no hesitancy in endorsing his statement. When the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) says the same thing, I have no reason to say that I am opposed to the idea. But,

let there be no mistake whatsoever, I am absolutely opposed to the method being used to put this bill through. When I said in a few words this afternoon that I thought this was a government-sponsored private bill, I was hearing the voice of experience. I believed everything I said at that time, whether you did or not, Mr. Speaker; and I am surprised that public opinion is not aroused in this country at the suggestion that this great natural resource should be-and I am going to use tl)e word-exploited. That is what you are going to do. Rarely, if ever, Mr. Speaker, will you find me reading a speech or a quotation to Canada's House of Commons; but I have here a clipping which makes me feel that I could talk on all through the night against this particular bill and its twin brother, the one which was postponed for a little while, when I find that pipe line bonds jumped from $100 in share value to $300. The heading of the article is "Without Precedent in Market History, Pipe Lines at $300." Must I read that whole article? No, I do not read anything in the House of Commons if I can avoid it. But here are a group of men sitting behind mahogany desks, in mahogany chairs, going to exploit this proposition. I will give you the reference. You can read it for yourselves and draw your own conclusions. It is dated March 25, published in a Toronto paper, under the heading "Trends and Prospects in Field of Enterprise, in Oil". I will not mention the name. Get the quotation yourselves. They are a responsible firm. What a clean-up they are going to make on these pipe line securities. I have not time to put it all on the record. Somebody else can do it. I have a great deal more I want to say. It reads in part:
Bond trading during the past week was marked by fractional easing in prices of a number of Dominion of Canada high-grade issues ... A total of $29,500,000 . . . the largest of these, $20 million.
Then it goes on:
An issue of Canadian Western Natural Gas Company ?8 million 3J per cent debentures due April 1, 1971, will early next week be offered at par . . .
And in the heading it is stated that the price has moved up to $300. You will always have that sort of trading, Mr. Speaker. You will always have people who will live by their wits. That group is perhaps only one out of a hundred. The rest of us will plow a lonely furrow or we shall earn our money so that it makes it easy for us to sleep at nights. It is my high privilege to be doing that now in Alberta, in Calgary, burning natural gas. I was privileged to start two enterprises there. Neither of them has made a dollar yet but they will for the future generations that my good friend the hon. member from Victoria, Ontario (Mr. Hodgson) was

talking about. In the meantime we have a vision of what Alberta and British Columbia mean to the Anglo-Saxon race.
Sitting with me in the Savoy hotel some three or four years ago were some Englishmen. We decided that we would start these enterprises. One of the reasons was that fuel was cheap and that we could get help there.
I have in front of me the financial statement of the Canadian Organic Development Limited. It is my high honour to be the president of it and its subsidiaries. I find that the judgment which was used some four years ago in London, England, may not have been as sound as it might be. I notice here a red figure of $271,683.52 for one organization; $111,592.22 in red figures in the other; and $29,768 in red in the third. There is a credit balance of $13,945 in Edmonton. But that does not matter. We have faith in Alberta; we have faith in British Columbia.
I know what I am talking about, Mr. Speaker. There is no place in the world where fuel is as cheap. As you who are in business know, fuel comprises anywhere from 20 per cent to 40 per cent of the cost of production. There is no other place in the world where fuel can be found which is as cheap as in Alberta. I plead with the house. I use the words of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier). He pleaded with the house. Let some of the rest of us plead with the house that we keep these natural resources in this country, and bring here people who will develop them. How are they going to do it? It was my privilege to ride by plane over the pipe lines of Iraq and Iran, to see the sand, the desert and what not; and in the same period to see what pumping water on the sand accomplishes. I saw that it would grow almost anything. Let me give you one example. I saw it in Mildura, Australia, where water was brought to the sand. As soon as it was brought from the Thomson river, the area which was irrigated supplied half the world with raisins and currants. I saw the camels in Nigeria go round and round. They brought buckets and buckets of water. I saw the grapes and tasted the wine made from the grapes that were produced on that soil. I am thinking of British Columbia. I am thinking of those irrigated areas such as we have seen in the Kootenay valley. I am thinking of the other irrigation schemes that some hon. members have in the backs of their minds.
I am thinking of the dreams of the previous member for Davenport, who visualized what might be done for western Canada if water were brought to those areas where the sand blows so often, and how it might be irrigated. I am thinking of the oil and gas so close to
Alberta Natural Gas Company Lethbridge, which might be used for pumping water to irrigate that area, for generations to come. I am thinking of the sandstorm over which I flew over Lethbridge a couple of years ago. We had to go so high to get away from that sandstorm, and finally we had to land in Calgary and go back by train. I am thinking of the oil in Calgary. I am thinking of the oil and gas which might be used not only for irrigation of those provinces but to pump water to irrigate Kelowna and Penticton. I can remember most of them, but I am not going to take the time to repeat them to the house. There are a lot of them out there that need water for irrigation, but they need gas and oil to pump the water to where they want it when they cannot get enough from the mountainside. I am thinking that one and all should pause before we give away our birthright for a mess of pottage.
Oh, oh.

Someone chuckles. I am very serious in what I say. My hon. friend from Ontario has not got a monopoly on things even if he happens to have nine children. A grandchild of mine was born yesterday, and I am thinking of our youth when they come along.
I hope he is going to be a Liberal.

He is fairly liberal at twelve pounds, but apart from that the last word that I have had is that he is quite all right. We have to think of them. This is no idle chatter. If some of you younger members will look at the statistics you will find out for yourselves that there are more Canadians in the United States than there are in Canada. That information might make you stop and think a little bit. Even though we have a cold northern climate I say in the same sentence that there is no country in the world that offers greater opportunities than Canada. I have been round the world except for Japan and China. You can have them. I have got behind the iron curtain only once, and I do not want to get behind it again. But no matter where I have been, I tell you I cannot visualize in my most quiet moments any better opportunity than we have in this country.
I ask this simple question: If you are going to take care and be responsible for those opportunities, what are you going to do about those God-given resources that are at your elbow? Are hon. members going to sit in this chamber and let their constituents be hewers of wood and drawers of water for people south of the border just because they have some high-priced money or United States dollars? Or are you going to be men

Alberta Natural Gas Company and not mice and rise in your places and say to the rest of the world, "We are a strong nation; we are going to develop our resources; we are going to keep that gas and oil in Alberta and British Columbia." Some of my family are there now. If I were not so enthusiastic about my home town, as every young man is as a rule, I would like to transport right into Alberta well over a million dollars' worth of bricks and mortar on which I am not making a dollar at this time in Ontario. That is where I would go. A poet said "Give me back my youth". I would love to have some of it back, and Alberta and British Columbia would be my destination if I had to make a living, Mr. Speaker. I look forward to the day when these ideas, if they are worth anything, will grip the imagination of my friends. I heard an hon. member from Quebec province make a very brilliant speech today in French. Let the possibilities of these provinces grip the imagination of his own people in Quebec. Let them grip the imagination of my people, not only in Ontario, but also in the old land. Let us go out and take hold of these two provinces, with all their potentialities, and give nothing away. Let us hang on to it and let us develop that country, because the possibilities are there. Then, when your day comes to sign off, you will be able to say that you have done a good job. I am glad to be able to look back twenty years and to say that that is where the possibilities are. Let us keep them for our Canadian people. Let us have a pipe line worthy of the trust Providence has placed in us, when we were entrusted with all these natural resources.

Mr. Speaker, today I wish to say a few words in connection with this bill. First of all I am anxious to put on record the opinions of constituted bodies, municipal and civil, in British Columbia who have been studying this problem and who have been wondering about the action their representatives in the House of Commons will take.
I am pleased that we are having the opportunity to discuss this bill further, because I believe we can throw some additional light upon what has already been said. Then, when the various members go to their constituencies during the Easter recess, they will be able to explain to them the benefits which will accrue to Canada if this line is routed through Canada and becomes an all-Canadian route. They will be able to show to their constituents the great possibilities in the development of our western country. Therefore I welcome this opportunity of speaking with respect to the bill for the first time before the Easter recess.
[Mr. Harris (Danforth.l
First of all, however, I should like to place on record the opinion held by the city council of Vancouver. Hon. members will have heard in previous speeches the opinion expressed unanimously by the legislature of British Columbia. Now we come to the great metropolitan area of Vancouver. The Vancouver city council on March 27, 1950, just a week ago today, passed this resolution:
That the city council advise the federal government of its opinion that the routing of a gas pipe line through British Columbia is imperative for the industrial development of the regional area through Vancouver.
Apparently that resolution was sent to the government. However, as this is not a government bill-although perhaps one might be excused for thinking that it is-it is possible that private members who do not represent British Columbia constituencies might not have had a copy of the resolution. It is for that reason that I am anxious to place it on the record.
I have in my hand a resolution passed by the Vancouver-New Westminster and district trades and labour council. This resolution, dated March 30, reads in this way:
Whereas an all-Canadian route for the proposed natural gas pipe line from Alberta to British Columbia will help control the gas in Canada until most Canadians have first been served and
Whereas more employment will result in Canada, both from construction and future maintenance than any other proposed route
Therefore be it resolved that this Vancouver-New Westminster and district trades and labour council strongly urge the dominion government to authorize the proposed all-Canadian route.
Another labour council which is very directly interested, the metal trades council of Vancouver, New Westminster and district, through a brief, states that it admires the persistent efforts which are being made by certain British Columbian members to route the pipe line through British Columbia. They go on to say:
Our delegates and members support you in the efforts which are being made to have this line routed through British Columbia. We earnestly request the continued support and favourable assistance to any company favouring a pipe line through British Columbia.
Then, to show the similarity between the views expressed by the great metropolitan areas and those of the smaller communities, I will now quote the view of the small community of Rutland. Their board of trade, which has a motto the first two words of which are "Be loyal", passed this resolution:
Resolved that this meeting of the Rutland board of trade go on record as being opposed to the natural gas pipe line going through the United States to Vancouver, and urge rhe support of the British Columbia members of parliament be given to the plan of routing the line through British Columbia.

There you have the recommendations from the municipal authorities in the cities, the labour councils, those who are closest in touch with the labour situation, urging that from the point of view of providing labour for Canadians these pipe lines be routed through British Columbia. Finally we have one of many small municipalities, which might be along the route, urging that the all-Canadian route be followed.
All those organizations are anxious to have this great Canadian resource made available for Canadians. At this time I do not intend to elaborate upon that point, nor do I intend to deal with the matter of these pipe lines going through British Columbia from a national defence point of view, as I did a few weeks ago when we were discussing another bill. Everything I said on that bill is applicable to the one we are discussing tonight.
Reference was made by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) to the remarks of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Gibson) in which, if I understood the hon. member for Kootenay West correctly, he intimated that the hon. member for Comox-Alberni was not interested in these problems, or had said he was not interested in these problems, because he represented a Vancouver island constituency and that it was not possible to convey the gas and oil across the straits of Georgia to the gulf islands and to Vancouver island. If the pipe line was routed through British Columbia to Vancouver it would be practical to carry it across these inland waters. The waters are sheltered by Vancouver island and no severe storms occur in that area. Then Nanaimo, Victoria and other points on Vancouver island could be served.
Apparently certain hon. members who have spoken did not think that this could be done. The hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Gibson) seemed to be hesitant and did not think it worth while routing the line through British Columbia. I am not an engineer and therefore cannot speak with personal knowledge regarding the feasibility of carrying a pipe line under water so with your permission I should like to read to the house a detailed account of Operation Pluto which I am sure will be of interest to hon. members. Just after D-day it was found essential to pipe across the English channel petrol, as it is called in the army, to supply the forces operating in northwest Europe. After an exhaustive examination it was found practical to put a pipe line under the English channel. If a pipe line could be constructed under the English channel then it should be feasible to construct one under the strait of Georgia so that the residents of Vancouver island might
Alberta Natural Gas Company have the benefit of Alberta gas provided it were piped through British Columbia to Vancouver. I am going to quote from Kees-ing's Contemporary Archives dated June 23-30, 1945, page 7273:
United Kingdom-British wartime engineering and scientific departments. Allied expeditionary force supplied by petrol by cross-channel pipe line- (Operation Pluto).
Particulars, hitherto withheld for security reasons, were recently released of important British engineering and scientific developments in connection with the war.
It was announced on May 24 that a large part of the allied expeditionary force had] been supplied with petrol by an under-water pipe line system stretching across the channel to the continent. An account of this operation, known as "Operation Pluto" (pipe line under the ocean) and wholly British in conception, is given below.
The scheme originated in April, 1942, when Admiral Mountbatten (then chief of combined operations) asked the petroleum warfare department whether it would be possible to lay a pipe line across the channel in order to guarantee the uninterrupted delivery of millions of gallons of petrol, normally requiring special harbour, dock and storage facilities, at times and places needed. Experts considered this impossible, but some days later, Mr. A. C. Hartley (chief engineer, Anglo-Iranian Petroleum Company) suggested the laying from cable ships of a pipe line resembling a submarine electric power cable without the core and insulation. Within a fortnight several hundred yards of this pipe line (later known as "Hais" Hartley-Anglo-Iranian-Siemens) had been produced by Messrs. Siemens Brothers Limited and laid in the Thames, with such promising results that Mr. Lloyd (secretary for petroleum) was instructed by Mr. Churchill to press ahead with the scheme. In December, 1942, an experimental cable was laid between Swansea and Ilfracombe, where currents and conditions approximated most nearly to those of the English channel, and for over a year consumers in north Devon and Cornwall were supplied with petrol without knowing that it had been pumped across the Bristol channel.
Meanwhile a second proposal had been made at the end of April, 1942, by Mr. B. G. Ellis (chief oil fields engineer, Burmah Oil Company) and Mr. H. A. Hammick (chief engineer, Iraq Petroleum Company), who suggested that three-inch diameter steel piping might be used by welding together 20-foot sections into the required lengths and winding on a drum. It being demonstrated that from drums of 30 feet or more in diameter it could be wound relatively straight.
When you get through with that read Dun and Bradstreet's.
Will the hon. member let me have the article he wants me to read from?
I will send you down a copy tomorrow.

I am sorry I should have been interrupted because I thought hon. members would be interested in this. I continue to quote:
After the building of a factory to weld "Hamel" piping (Hammick-Ellis) into 4,000 foot lengths, with storage facilities for 350 miles, the Admiralty converted a hopper barge into a craft (named H.M.S.

Alberta Natural Gas Company
Persephone) with a "great wheel" rotating in trunnions on deck, capable of carrying many miles of piping and paying it into the sea. This was followed by a second idea, the construction of a giant floating drum capable of carrying the full length for the channel crossing, tests at the national physical laboratory, Teddington, showing that this could be towed like a large bobbin, paying off pipe as it went. Arrangements were made for mooring the drums, known as "Conundrums" ("Conuns") in deep water at the end of the pipe racks to enable the 4,000 foot lengths to be welded into a continuous length of 30 or more miles and wound on the "Conuns" while they were rotated. After successful trials, the manufacture of "Hais" cable and "Hamel" pipe was arranged, and the petroleum war department (Director-General, Major-General Sir Donald Banks) was made responsible for the whole scheme, including the provision of pumping stations.
"Force Pluto", numbering 1,100 officers and men under Captain F. J. Hutchings, with vessels ranging from 10,000 ton ships to barges and motorboats, was then formed; six "Conuns" constructed, each 90 feet long and over 50 feet in over-all diameter (the drums themselves being 60 feet by 40 feet), carrying 70 miles of pipe line and weighing 1,600 tons; new pipe lines run from the British system (extended north to special tanker discharging berths at Brom-borough dock, near Birkenhead) to the coast, making 1,000 miles in all; and high power pumping stations built and camouflaged in an old fort and amusement park, seaside bungalows, etc. Shortly before "D-day" the arrangements were inspected by Mr. Churchill (who had kept in close touch with all developments, and whose decision that the scheme should be pressed forward had ensured close interdepartmental co-operation and priority in materials), Mr. Lloyd, and the late Admiral Sir Bertram Ramsay.
Operation Pluto began a few weeks after "D-day", as soon as the approaches to the tip of the Cherbourg peninsula had been cleared of mines. Several lines were established, and on August 12 a special petroleum unit of the R.A.S.C. began pumping petrol from the isle of Wight to Normandy, maintaining close contact with Cherbourg by wireless telephone, so as to detect instantly any variation in the quantity delivered. It soon became necessary, however, to establish lines across the narrow part of the channel in order to avoid the strain of supplying the advancing allied armies from Cherbourg. As soon as Boulogne was captured, and mines cleared, pipe lines were laid from Dungeness to Boulogne, bringing the oil 200 miles nearer the front. The Royal Engineers then built and the R.A.S.C. operated a continually lengthening system from Boulogne to Antwerp . . . and eventually across the Rhine, enabling over one million gallons daily (sufficient for the entire needs of the 21st army group) to be pumped through to Germany, other lines being subsequently laid from Cherbourg to Frankfurt for the use of the American army. In all, twenty pipe lines were laid across the channel (four or five to Cherbourg and fifteen or sixteen, totalling 500 miles, to Boulogne), many operations taking place under adverse weather conditions and strong tides. "Operation Pluto" achieved complete surprise and even the "Conuns" sailed unscathed across the channel, the enemy assuming them to be not worth attention. By the end of the war in Europe 120 million gallons had been pumped through to Germany, ten cable and six steel pipe lines being continued in operation thereafter for the use of the allied armies of occupation.
I thought this would be of interest to many hon. members. Not only is it worth while putting it on record as a glorious achievement and demonstration of the skill of the engineers, but it demonstrates the practicability of
(Mr. Pearkes.]
piping gas and oil from the city of Vancouver over to Vancouver island in order that the people of the island might have the opportunity of utilizing the surplus gas available in the Alberta fields. I think it is generally known that the commission appointed by the Alberta government in 1948 found that at that time there was an abundance of surplus gas, having regard to the foreseeable requirements of Alberta for many years to come.
Since 1948 new fields have been discovered. The Leduc field has come into operation, and also the Redwater field. Many others are being developed in northern Alberta. The result is it is estimated that the surpluses available today in Alberta are three times what they were just a few years ago. We know that the premier of Alberta has announced that, provided the long-range requirements of the people of his province are safeguarded, it is the policy of the Alberta government to allow gas to be exported from that province. Without going into the particular details, we know that a bill was passed a year ago granting a charter to a company which has intimated that it will follow an allCanadian route. The two bills which are before us at the present time contain no assurance that the gas will be transported by an all-Canadian route to the Pacific coast. In fact, I think it is no secret that the directors of these companies have intimated that they will transport the gas through the southern part of Alberta into the United States to supply the great cities of Spokane, Wenatchee, Seattle, Portland, and so on. They have intimated that what has been referred to as a stub line will be extended to Vancouver in order to supply Vancouver so far as is practicable with whatever gas there may be left over. I understand that would be a longer and probably more expensive route than the one from Edmonton through Jasper, Yellow-head, Kamloops, and along the new provincial Hope road. I say longer because it would be longer from the centre of oil and gas activity. A few years ago the centre of that activity was in the southern part of Alberta. Gas fields were first discovered south of Calgary in the region of Purple Springs, Grassy Lake, Lethbridge, the Turner valley, and so on, but that centre of activity has moved northward.
Now, I do not think it is incorrect to say that it will probably be north and west of the city of Edmonton. If the route should be measured, therefore, from some point around Edson, west of Edmonton, through the Yel-lowhead pass, or coming down through Lethbridge, the gas will have to be gathered at some central point such as I have suggested. I understand that a company has been incorporated to gather the gas from the various

fields in Alberta. Then, if the Canadian route were followed it would be possible to tap in, perhaps west of Jasper somewhere, the fields which are being developed in the Peace river country. The extent of those fields has not yet been estimated, but there would appear to be enormous reserves there. It may be that by having a line from Prince George, Dawson Creek, and Fort St. James, some of those places, it would be possible to service the whole of the eastern side of British Columbia with oil and gas.
A difference between the two lines, which I think is quite striking, is that if the southern route were followed I believe there would only be a distance of some 150 miles of the pipe line in British Columbia. If the northern route were followed, then some 700 miles would be located in Canada. As pointed out by those resolutions which I read, the construction and maintenance of this line in Canada would give a tremendous amount of employment to Canadians, not only in the actual construction of the line, but in the preparation of such things as bridging materials. These bridging materials would be required for the construction and maintenance of the line. Then there would be a road paralleling the pipe line, no matter which direction the route followed. We want that northern part of central British Columbia developed. It is a wonderful country. I have been through it many times, and I know that there is untold wealth in that hinterland. I believe this pipe-line measure presents an opportunity whereby we can feel we are really making a contribution to the development of the province, or a part of the province, which at the moment is but sparsely populated.
There are unlimited possibilities for further development there, and I do hope that when members return to their constituencies, particularly those members from British Columbia who at the moment perhaps do not know the interior as well as they would like to know it, who have not grasped the enormous possibilities of that area, they will take advantage of the opportunity to see that district. They will find out how it can be developed, and how it can be given industries if these pipe lines go through that area.
Alberta Natural Gas Company I hope hon. members will seize the opportunity presented by the Easter recess to view that land, anid consult with their constituents as to whether they would like to have that line run through the northern part of British Columbia. I sincerely hope it will be possible to give the people of British Columbia the advantages of a pipe line from the Alberta fields to the British Columbia coast.

It was not until a short time ago that I decided to take part in this debate. I am sure that a debate such as this interests not only the people of British Columbia and western Canada, but also the people from the rest of Canada. I am satisfied that anyone listening to the member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) would realize that almost anything at all can be done with pipe lines. I feel sure the member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Maybank) will agree with me when I say that almost anything can be done with pipe lines.
